## The situation {.smaller}

Within days of the M7.5 quake (24 June 2026), **at least eight** organisations published
satellite building-damage maps — government (Copernicus), academic radar (OSU, IMPACT),
optical AI (Microsoft, U. Houston, WFP/LIST), debris models (UNEP), volunteer AI (HOT, DISHA).

They **disagreed with each other, sometimes wildly.** A coordinator receiving them in the
same week had no principled way to answer: *which do I trust, for what, and at what scale?*

::: {.tldr}
**What we did.** Scored the six products that published an analysed extent against **three
independent reference datasets whose blind spots don't overlap** — so they check each
other, and the products.
:::

::: {.tldr}
**Bottom line.** As delivered, most single products carried **less usable per-building
information than a no-satellite baseline**. But products *are* good at ranking
*neighbourhoods*, combining them helps (within limits), and the real leverage is **reference
quality + provider metadata transparency**.
:::

## Three questions we keep strictly separate

1. **Where is it worst?** — ranking neighbourhoods for triage.
2. **Which buildings?** — a per-building list you could send a crew to.
3. **What does everyone miss?** — including the "ground truth" itself.

And two performance frames we **never mix**:

- **Best case** — Caraballeda, the dense-damage coastal zone where **96% of the expert
  reference lives**. Flattering, and where most published numbers implicitly come from.
- **As delivered** — the whole product, every zone it shipped, junk included. What a
  responder actually received.

::: {.small}
Every number in this deck is tagged to one frame. That split is itself a finding.
:::

## The method: three references, three blind spots {.smaller}

| Reference | What it is | Can measure | **Cannot** measure |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Copernicus EMS** | expert analysts, VHR imagery | false alarms **and** misses | anything outside its mapped extents |
| **MapSwipe crowd** | 400+ volunteers, ~8,000 AI-flagged spots | false alarms | misses (only saw flagged places) |
| **ChatMap field** | 415 ground-reported damage points | misses | false alarms (positives only) |

Matching is **dual-anchored** (precision and recall from opposite anchors), so we never need
to count the vast stock of undamaged buildings. Radius **r = 10 m**, derived from the urban
fabric (median building spacing 9.7 m).

![](artefacts/RQ0-matching-basis/figs/fig_dual_anchor_matching.png)

## <span class="win">WIN</span> — products point at the right neighbourhoods

Per-building they're weak, but at **triage scale (~5 km²)** they correctly rank where it's
worst (rank correlation ρ ≈ 0.5–0.6; the residual errors track the **coast and shaking**,
not building density — a benign error structure that *preserves* ranking).

![](artefacts/RQ3-prioritization-error-structure/figs/rq3_priority_map.png)

::: {.small}
Best case (Caraballeda), neighbourhood scale. **This is what the products are genuinely good
for today: sector prioritisation, not per-building work orders.**
:::

## <span class="fail">FAIL</span> — per building, even at their best

In Caraballeda, where they score highest, per-building precision is **0.04–0.09**: for every
flag that lands on real (expert-recorded) damage, **ten to twenty do not.**

The benchmark that should worry us: a model given **only day-zero geography** — distance to
coast, building density, ShakeMap intensity, *all available before any satellite is tasked* —
matches the best single product.

![](artefacts/RQ8-learned-fusion/figs/rq8_geography_baseline.png)

## <span class="fail">FAIL harder</span> — as delivered, geography wins

Scored across everything each product actually shipped (not just its best zone), **five of
six products carried *less* building-level information than the no-satellite baseline.**

| Product | as-delivered precision | vs. day-zero baseline |
|---|---|---|
| Microsoft | 0.081 | ~ tie (only product to hold up) |
| OSU | 0.036 | **loses** (baseline 0.084) |
| IMPACT | 0.032 | **loses** (0.077) |
| UNEP | 0.027 | **loses** (0.076) |
| LIST | 0.026 | **loses** (0.076) |
| UH | 0.009 | **loses badly** (0.091) |

::: {.small}
Microsoft survives **because it only shipped its carefully-analysed coastal strip.**
Coverage *restraint* is itself a product virtue — UH shipping everywhere destroyed its own
precision. *(Caveat: outside Caraballeda the reference is thin; but a responder faced the
same information deficit.)*
:::

## The ground truth is itself half-blind

Scoring **Copernicus against the field reports**: it recorded **94% of completely destroyed**
buildings but only **49% of "significant" damage.** Every product shows the same slope.

![](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2e_grade_slope.png)

::: {.small}
Consequences: (1) satellite damage detection is really **destruction** detection —
shelter-damage needs are under-counted. (2) **Measured precision is a floor; measured
recall is a ceiling.** Crowd review lifts Microsoft's precision from 0.08 to ~0.24 — the gap
is in the *reference*, not the product.
:::

## The split, visualised: one product is many scorecards

![](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2i_per_aoi_scorecard.png)

::: {.small}
96% of reference damage is in Caraballeda (first column). Outside it, products keep flagging
at scale (UH: 32,000 flags in Santa Cruz) while measured precision collapses to 0.00–0.02 —
**though we cannot separate "product hallucination" from "reference too thin" there.** The
honest verdict: *every headline number describes dense-damage coastal terrain.*
:::

## Does combining products fix it? Honestly — partly

Requiring **agreement across products** trades precision against coverage. It turns an
unusable list into a **triage-usable** one — but **no rule is both cheap and complete.**

![](artefacts/RQ5-ensemble/figs/rq5c_operational_dial.png)

::: {.small}
Best case. Bars show the cost range (crowd-adjusted → expert-only). At ~4-of-6 you reach
**74% of damage at ~3–5 field visits per real find**; full agreement is nearly clean but
covers only a quarter. **This is a prioritisation dial, not a send-a-crew work order —**
and it's the honest ceiling of what fusion buys.
:::

## The hero story: transparency lets you fix failures

Microsoft's one bad zone (western strip) flagged **28.7% of buildings** — crowd validators
rejected **71% as undamaged.** We root-caused it **from Microsoft's own published metadata**:
that zone had a single satellite pass, processed by a per-scene model with no cross-check.

![](artefacts/RQ7-mapswipe-validation/figs/rq7_west_cluster_adjudication.png)

::: {.small}
**The point:** it was the *only* failure we could diagnose — because it was the *only*
product publishing per-building provenance. The other five fail undiagnosably. **Auditability
is a product property**, and the correction signal (the crowd campaign) existed within days
and reached no one.
:::

## What we'd recommend {.smaller}

::: {.tldr}
**Providers** — publish an analysed extent (non-negotiable); publish per-building provenance
(scene count + dates); *scope your coverage* rather than blanket-ship; clear a geography-only
baseline before release.
:::

::: {.tldr}
**Evaluators** — one expert reference under-counts light damage: publish precision as a
*floor*, or adjudicate against a second reference and publish an *interval*. Treat crowd and
field data as first-class, not afterthoughts.
:::

::: {.tldr}
**Responders** — trust the *area ranking*, not the building counts; set the agreement dial to
your own cost of a wasted visit vs. a missed building. Nothing here sees light damage
reliably — plan shelter assessments accordingly.
:::

## Where this is solid — and where it isn't

**Solid:** six products, three independent references, ~1,500 lines of reproducible open
code; the area-ranking win, the day-zero result, the per-zone collapse, and the west-cluster
diagnosis all replicate across frames.

**Honest limits:**

- **One event, one geography** (coastal, dense-urban); 96% of reference in one AOI.
- Outside Caraballeda the reference is too thin to cleanly separate product error from
  reference gaps — the as-delivered penalty leans on that.
- **No confidence intervals yet** — the ±0.01 gaps need them before we lean hard.
- The **timeliness axis** (accuracy × how fast each product arrived) is not yet built —
  arguably the most decision-relevant variable.

## The asks

::: {.ask}
**1. Back writing this up.** The framework (three-reference triangulation, the floor/ceiling
correction, the geography baseline as a validation bar) is novel and travels beyond this
event. It's a real contribution to how the sector evaluates these products.
:::

::: {.ask}
**2. Support taking findings to providers.** Constructive, evidence-based, and their own
metadata is the hero — this strengthens the ecosystem, doesn't just critique it.
:::

::: {.ask}
**3. Resource the two gaps that make it bulletproof:** confidence intervals, and the
timeliness axis (needs provider release dates — an ask we can make together).
:::

## {.smaller}

**Thank you.**

Working documents (internal): the findings register (`findings.qmd`, every result +
confidence + open flags) and the full manuscript draft (`manuscript_v2.qmd`). All figures
regenerate from frozen data via committed scripts.

::: {.small}
One-line summary to carry out of the room: *as delivered, most single damage products barely
beat a coastline-and-shakemap model; their value is in ranking areas and in combination, and
the biggest lever is better reference data and provider transparency — not better single
models.*
:::
